Outbreak Size

Latest analysis data cutoff: 30 August 2026. Page refreshed: 3 September 2026.

Beta

This page is in beta and still a work in progress. Please direct feedback to Collaboratory@who.int. This page is subject to the disclaimer below.

At a glance

Reported counts still understate true infections, but the gap has narrowed. The under-ascertainment ratio has fallen from roughly 0.3–2.4× against 1,031 suspected or confirmed cases on 27 May, to 1.5–3.2× against 6,100 confirmed cases on 15 August, based on a 90% credible interval of 9,088-19,366 cumulative infections. Eight separate analyses suggest persistent under-detection, with moderate confidence.

Multi-model estimates of cumulative Ebola outbreak size

Each colored point interval shows an individual model’s median (point) with 50%, 80%, and 95% uncertainty intervals. The grey band and line show a smoothed quantile-averaging ensemble (GAM spline fit to the 2.5th, 50th, and 97.5th percentiles across all models on a log10 scale).

Data: BDBV Modeling Hub model-output submissions, dated 18 May 2026–02 Sep 2026. Source: github.com/InsightNet-US/BDBV-Modeling-Hub

Synthesizing evidence¶

State of the evidence¶

Six peer-reviewed or pre-print outbreak-size estimation studies, plus two focused growth-dynamics analyses, span from 22 May to 30 August 2026.[1][2][3][4] The evidence base is growing and diverse in approach. Methods include back-calculation from deaths, travel-based geographic spread, branching process projections, joint Bayesian renewal models, metapopulation transmission models, SEIRD scenario ensembles, and growth-rate estimation. However, comparability is limited by differing data cutoff dates, varying geographic scopes (Ituri alone versus DRC-wide), and divergent framing. Most analyses address detected or projected confirmed cases, while only a subset produce explicit estimates of undetected infections at a single cutoff.

How the estimates compare¶

McCabe et al., working with data through 27 May, combine back-calculation from deaths and geographic spread to estimate 280–2,520 total BVD cases in DRC.[5] Against the 1,031 suspected or confirmed cases reported as of that date, this suggests a ratio of 0.3–2.4×. That denominator includes suspected cases that may not be Bundibugyo infections, so this ratio is not directly comparable to a true-to-confirmed detection multiplier.[6] Abbott et al., using data through 30 August with a more complex joint Bayesian model, estimate 9,088–19,366 cumulative infections (90% credible interval) against 6,100 confirmed cases, implying a detection multiplier of 1.5–3.2×.[7] Kim et al., refining the geographic spread method to account for healthcare-seeking travel, report detection-multiplier estimates that depend on whether healthcare-seeking cases are included; excluding them, they produce informative upper bounds for burden but do not recover a central multiplier.[8][9] Epistorm’s metapopulation model, calibrated to 717 confirmed cases in Ituri Province on 13 June, allows ascertainment as low as 20%, implying up to a 5× multiplier, although the model does not report this explicitly.[2] Chamla et al., working with 598 confirmed cases as of 8 June, deliberately set reporting fraction to 1.0 and therefore do not estimate a separate true-case count; their analysis tracks confirmed-case trajectories under three transmissibility scenarios rather than estimating under-detection.[10]

These figures should not be read as a time trend in the detection multiplier. Scopes, dates, and estimands differ across analyses, so the sequence reflects different questions answered with different data rather than repeated application of one method to a moving outbreak.

Verheyden and Mudogo do not produce a detection multiplier but instead quantify the pre-detection growth implied by the confirmed case series. At a doubling time of 5.5 days, the 25-day detection lag corresponds to approximately six-fold case amplification before international response mechanisms engaged. By declaration on 15 May, the model implies 20–38 circulating cases (median 28) against 378 confirmed cases reported as of 2 June, describing a different quantity than a detection ratio at a fixed cutoff.[11][12]

The spread in estimates reflects three main sources of divergence. First, data quality improved substantially and discontinuously on 28 May, when DRC restructured case-finding and laboratory deployment; analyses using pre-discontinuity data see slower, steadier growth, while later analyses see faster confirmed-case escalation and a lower multiplier in relative terms. Second, methods differ in how they handle ascertainment. Back-calculation from deaths assumes a CFR and applies it to estimated death counts; geographic spread works backward from exported cases; and renewal models estimate ascertainment directly from surveillance data. Third, geographic scope matters. Ituri Province estimates differ from DRC-wide estimates, and analyses that model Nord Kivu as a secondary focus versus analyses that exclude it generate divergent case-size estimates.

Key uncertainties and assumptions¶

Across analyses, three uncertainties drive nearly all divergence and would shift all estimates together if resolved.

The first is the ascertainment fraction itself, the proportion of infections that surveillance detects and reports as confirmed. Most analyses assume ascertainment between 20% and 100%, a ten-fold band encompassing the entire plausible range.[2][10] The choice of floor matters enormously. Abbott et al.'s joint model yields credible intervals that tighten substantially as the ascertainment floor rises from 10% to 20% to 30%, and Kim et al.'s upper-bound analysis becomes directly uninformative if all cases are assumed confirmed.[9] Earlier analyses, constrained to small numerators (three exported cases for McCabe et al.'s travel-based method), were forced to bracket uncertainty through scenario analysis rather than fit it; later analyses, working with larger confirmed-case series, can estimate ascertainment but do so under model assumptions that may not hold.

The second shared uncertainty is the epidemic doubling time in the early phase. Verheyden and Mudogo’s growth-dynamics analysis estimates a 5.5-day doubling time (95% CI 4.2–7.8 days), roughly three times faster than prior BDBV outbreaks.[13] Epistorm, Chamla et al., and Abbott et al. all use slightly longer doubling times (10.6–11.7 days in their posteriors), reflecting different fitting windows and calibration strategies.[14][15][16] This matters because at exponential growth, a 5.5-day doubling time versus an 11.7-day doubling time implies roughly a four-fold difference in case count at any fixed date before response controls took effect. Which doubling time is correct depends on when the calibration window starts. Pre-28 May data show faster growth; post-28 May data show slower growth, reflecting both response scale-up and declining transmission growth.

The third shared uncertainty is the case fatality ratio and its trajectory. McCabe et al. fixed CFR at 33% from prior outbreaks; Verheyden and Mudogo documented a rise from 12% to 44% and attributed it to ascertainment lag rather than virulence; Abbott et al. estimated a posterior CFR of 35–58% (90% CI); Chamla et al. drew CFR from a uniform distribution (15–25%).[17][18][19][20] Back-calculation from deaths is particularly sensitive to this parameter, since multiplying estimated deaths by the reciprocal of CFR produces the case count. Early uncertainty about true mortality (confirmed versus suspected deaths) was substantial; as of 21 May, the confirmed CFR (10.8%) diverged markedly from suspected cases (23.6%), and this discrepancy drove different inferences about outbreak magnitude depending on whether analysts weighted confirmed or suspected deaths more heavily.

Beyond these three, Abbott et al. flag two features of their own model mechanics that widen or distort the reported uncertainty. Later situation reports revise earlier totals up or down as suspects are reclassified and newly-reporting health zones are added, and this revision process is not modelled.[21] The surveillance streams are fitted as conditionally independent given latent incidence, yet they observe overlapping people, which can understate uncertainty, and whether the streams imply mutually consistent outbreak sizes is not assessed.[22]

Two additional structural assumptions are shared. The first is a single zoonotic spillover event (rather than ongoing animal-to-human spillover), and the second is no spatial structure beyond an Ituri/Nord Kivu split. These are reasonable first-order approximations but may mask early supposition of subclinical circulation or structured geographic heterogeneity that would affect estimates. None of the analyses relax these assumptions in sensitivity analyses.

What would reduce uncertainty¶

Two additions would have a substantial impact on current understanding.

The first, and most important, is higher-frequency line-list data. Records with symptom-onset dates, confirmation dates, death dates, and care-setting indicators would enable direct estimation of CFR by setting, lag distributions by severity, and ascertainment curves over time, replacing the current reliance on aggregate surveillance counts and scenario assumptions. This single data source would anchor nearly all downstream estimates. Chamla et al., Verheyden and Mudogo, and Abbott et al. all flag line-list data as the critical missing input.[23][24][25] As of late July, these data remain incomplete.

The second is contemporaneous validation of cross-border mobility patterns and detection sensitivity at Uganda’s points of entry. McCabe et al.'s travel-based method rests on point-of-entry volume estimates that may have been unrepresentative during the early pre-declaration weeks, and Kim et al. document that all imported cases were healthcare-seeking travellers, a selection that violates the method’s core assumption.[26][27] Direct measurement of border crossing volumes, travel-while-symptomatic rates, and Uganda’s detection sensitivity during the May 2026 window would tighten the range of the travel-based estimates. Kim et al. identify this gap explicitly and call for enhanced border surveillance data infrastructure to resolve it in future outbreaks.[28]

Open questions¶

Multiple analyses name specific unresolved questions that follow from data gaps rather than model limitations.

McCabe et al. call for urgent characterisation of the outbreak’s size, growth rate, and geographical extent as soon as possible, flagging both epidemiological case time series and genomic data as crucial inputs.[29] Mooring et al. emphasise that high-quality time series of case and death counts are essential to more precisely estimate R0.[30] Kim et al. underscore the need for better understanding of cross-border dynamics and household transmission patterns to refine geographic spread estimates.[28][31] Chamla et al. flag contact-tracing data as notably scarce and call for iterative recalibration as new data emerge.[32][33] Verheyden and Mudogo raise the question of an earlier, undetected cluster in Mongbwalu health zone, positioning a back-calculation range from early February to mid-April as a plausibility bound pending independent verification.[34]

What this means for the response¶

The evidence suggests that the confirmed case count as of late May 2026 substantially understated the true outbreak size at that moment, with a likely detection multiplier of 1–5× and a plausible upper bound closer to 10×, though the evidence for any single point multiplier is weak. Confirmed counts should be treated as a lower bound on burden, committed care needs, and transmission potential. Operationally, this reading has three implications.

First, surveillance capacity was the rate-limiting step through May and into early June. A 28 May 2026 discontinuity in case reporting, externally corroborated by a documented Africa CDC capacity-expansion plan, marked the moment case-finding began catching up to transmission. Before that date, the confirmed count substantially lagged the true outbreak size. After that date, the detection gap narrowed. Response teams should expect that improved surveillance drives apparent case increases that reflect detection, not acceleration of underlying transmission, a distinction that shapes both resource-planning timelines and communication strategy.

Second, the 5.5-day doubling time in the early phase means response delays carry exponential cost. Verheyden and Mudogo document that pre-international-alert transmission lasted approximately 16 days, corresponding to roughly six-fold undetected case growth; each additional week of delay before high isolation coverage was achieved doubled the case burden further.[35]

Third, the evidence suggests that neither laboratory confirmation nor suspected-case tallies on their own provide an operationally adequate view of outbreak size during early phases. Combining signal from multiple surveillance streams, confirmed, suspected, healthcare-worker cases, points of entry, and retrospective death investigations, and integrating across streams using ensemble or hierarchical methods, as Abbott et al. demonstrate, produces narrower credible intervals and better-calibrated uncertainty than any single stream alone.[36] Operational teams should adopt multi-stream surveillance dashboards that reflect the most recent joint estimate, refreshed daily, rather than tracking confirmed counts in isolation.

Abbott et al. (30 Aug 2026)
Estimating the current size of the 2026 DRC Bundibugyo virus outbreak¶

Read the analysis

Overview¶

This is a live, continuously updated Bayesian model that tries to estimate the true number of BVD infections in DRC to date, including those never reported or confirmed by surveillance. It is a real-time joint Bayesian estimate of the current size of that outbreak, refreshed as new data arrive, since most infections are not yet reported and the current size has to be inferred from the surveillance data that are available.[37] The model is a discrete-time renewal process on a daily grid that fits in a single posterior the daily counts the INSP situation reports publish, including the suspected and confirmed case and death series as well as the laboratory, isolation, treatment-centre and recovery records.[36] The headline finding is that the outbreak is estimated to have caused roughly 9,088 to 19,366 infections to date (90% credible interval), which against the 6,100 laboratory-confirmed cases by the cut-off is roughly 1.5–3.2× as many infections, so confirmed cases are estimated to capture only a small share of the outbreak.[7]

Estimate¶

The headline (joint model) estimate of cumulative infections to date in DRC, at the 30 August 2026 cutoff, is 11,666-14,055 infections (30% credible interval), 10,622-15,716 (60%), and 9,088-19,366 (90%)[38]. Against the 6,100 laboratory-confirmed cases by the cut-off that is roughly 1.5-3.2× as many infections, so confirmed cases are estimated to capture only a small share of the outbreak.[39] The analysis also fits single-stream models (exports-only, deaths-only, cases-only, confirmed-only, onsets-only) so each stream’s own implied outbreak size can be compared with the joint posterior, but the specific numeric outputs of those individual-stream fits are not given in the visible text (they are exported to a separate data file rather than stated in prose). The document also describes frozen re-fits and comparisons against McCabe et al. and Chamla et al. scenario estimates as external sense-checks, but does not state the resulting comparison figures in the text provided.

Methods¶

Joint Bayesian renewal model: The headline method is a discrete-time renewal process on a daily grid that fits in a single posterior the daily counts the INSP situation reports publish, including the suspected and confirmed case and death series as well as the laboratory, isolation, treatment-centre and recovery records[36], together with a digitised epidemic curve by symptom-onset date and data on initial exports of cases and deaths to Uganda, taken from WHO situation reports and Disease Outbreak News[40], plus a genetic bound on the time to the most recent common ancestor and priors from the McCabe et al. report[41]. It produces a posterior over the infections and deaths to date, reported and unreported, the time-varying reproduction number with its growth rate and doubling time, the case-fatality ratio, and the ascertainment of each surveillance system[42]. This is described as a real-time joint Bayesian estimate of the current outbreak size, fitted to more of the available data streams than the original[43] McCabe et al. report, applied to DRC nationally with the Uganda export streams as a secondary track.

Single-stream models: Alongside the joint model, single-stream models are fit for each count-based stream (exported cases, suspected deaths, suspected cases, laboratory-confirmed cases, confirmed deaths, deaths among exports and the symptom-onset reporting triangle), so that each stream’s posterior over the outbreak size can be compared with the joint.[44] This is a diagnostic exercise applied to the same DRC national and Uganda export data as the joint model.

Genetic seeding sub-model: A separate component uses a BEAST time tree of the first ten sequenced genomes, placing the TMRCA... at a mean of 25 March 2026[45], treated as a one-sided seeding bound rather than a point estimate[46] to inform the cryptic pre-detection growth phase; this applies to the outbreak origin generally rather than a specific sub-national geography, since the sampled tree is almost entirely from Bunia.[47]

Frozen re-fits and comparisons with prior work: The frozen re-fit cuts the data to an earlier cut-off and re-fits the joint model, so that a change driven by newer data can be distinguished from one driven by a change of method.[48] The model is set beside the McCabe et al. scenario estimates as an external sense-check, matched in time at the cut-off each scenario was computed[49], and a forward projection from a frozen fit is also set against the Chamla et al. confirmed-case projection and the data observed since.[50]

Assumptions¶

Generation interval and incubation period: The generation interval is assumed Gamma-distributed with shape and scale taken from the Ebola virus disease serial interval used as a generation-time proxy (mean 15.3 d, SD 9.3 d; WHO Ebola Response Team 2014)[51]. The incubation period uses the Bundibugyo virus estimate from the 2007 Uganda outbreak (mean 6.3 d, 95% CI 5.2-7.3), with the mean prior reproducing that CI, but the source reports no interval on the spread so the SD prior is the analysts’ own choice.[52]

Onset-to-report and onset-to-death delays: A Bayesian reanalysis of the 2012 Isiro Bundibugyo virus outbreak line list is used to take the onset-to-admission delay as a Gamma with priors centred on the reanalysis posterior (implied mean about 4 d)[53], replacing McCabe et al.'s point-estimate approach, which fit a distributed delay from the same line list[54]. The reanalysis instead fits onset-to-death as two atomic Gamma components (onset-to-admission and admission-to-death) convolved together, giving an implied mean of about 13 d.[55]

Case-fatality ratio: Based on the CDC figure and a companion reanalysis baseline for non-healthcare-worker confirmed cases, a Beta prior is used with mean and interval matching the CDC figure and the corrected central CFR in the 20 May McCabe et al. report.[56] The posterior narrows to 0.35-0.58 (90% CI)[19].

Ascertainment: The DRC and Uganda ascertainment fractions share a logit-scale hyperprior centred on a reporting fraction of 0.75, reflecting the active case-finding of a declared Ebola response rather than baseline passive surveillance.[57]

Molecular clock and genetic seeding bound: The temporal sampling range is too short to estimate the molecular clock, so it is fixed to the substitutions/site/year rate of the 2013-2016 West African Ebola epidemic (Holmes et al., 2016).[58] Using the genetic TMRCA as a one-sided seeding bound rather than a point estimate follows a suggestion of N. Ferguson.[46] The clock is fixed and cross-outbreak or clock uncertainty is not propagated.[59]

Growth-rate/doubling-time prior: The growth rate carries a log-normal prior on the doubling time centred on 11.7 d from the BEAST X genomic reanalysis, with a wider log spread than that HPD implies, since the HPD is conditional on a single-rate coalescent assumption the field epidemiology contradicts.[60] An independent reanalysis puts the doubling time at 15.2-24.5 d, and the model’s own 95% interval on the doubling time (5.3-25.6 d) is set wide enough to contain both ranges.[61]

Structural assumptions - single seed, no spatial structure: The outbreak is assumed to have started from a single seed case introduced by a zoonotic spillover, growing deterministically through an unobserved cryptic exponential phase before sustained transmission was established.[62][63] The model inherits McCabe et al.'s epidemiological assumptions: a single zoonotic seed, an assumed generation interval, no spatial structure beyond the Ituri/Nord Kivu split, and no depletion of susceptibles.[64]

Cross-border travel and source population: The Ituri-side daily traveller total is a sample mean across roughly point-of-entry-weeks from McCabe et al. Table 3, used as a Normal prior, while the source population is kept fixed at the census value.[65]

Stream independence: The data streams are fitted as conditionally independent given latent incidence but observe overlapping people, which can understate uncertainty; whether the streams imply mutually consistent outbreak sizes is not assessed here.[66]

Limitations¶

Reliance on weakly-informed priors: Nearly all of the delays, the case-fatality ratio and the laboratory assumptions are set by priors informed at best by a handful of literature sources, often from other outbreaks, and in places reflect the authors’ own judgement rather than data from this outbreak; the data do little to move them, so these posteriors largely track their priors.[67]

Weak epidemiological timing signal and aggregate data: There are no counts by symptom onset or any other epidemiologically relevant date, only cumulative totals at the report date, so the timing of the underlying epidemic is weakly identified and recovered only through the assumed delays.[25]

Data sources¶

Primary outbreak data: DRC data come from the situation reports of the Institut National de Santé Publique, each giving national cumulative suspected cases and deaths, laboratory-confirmed cases and deaths, and specimens received and analysed by the laboratory, at the report date.[68] Key counts at their respective observation dates include suspected cases: 1,077 (26 May 2026)[69], suspected deaths: 246 (26 May 2026)[70], confirmed cases: 6,100 (30 August 2026)[71], confirmed deaths: 2,950 (30 August 2026)[72], and specimens analysed: 755 (28 May 2026)[73]. From 13 June the reports add a Tableau 6 patient-movement table for the treatment centres, read as daily admissions, in-care deaths, rule-outs and absconded flows.[74] Uganda data are the cases and the one death exported across the border, taken from the WHO situation reports and Disease Outbreak News[75], specifically 3 exported cases (23 May 2026)[76] and 1 export death (14 May 2026)[77]. From SitRep 059 (12 July) the situation reports also carry a raster figure of confirmed cases by symptom-onset date, digitised directly from the figure.[78]

Auxiliary data: Cross-border traveller volume and source population come from McCabe et al., with the source population fixed and the traveller volume given a Normal prior around the McCabe et al. figure[79] (daily outbound travellers prior mean 1,871, SD 200; source population 4,392,200[80]). A Bayesian reanalysis of the 2012 Isiro Bundibugyo virus outbreak line list[81] (originally Rosello et al. 2015) supplies onset-to-admission and onset-to-death delay estimates. The Bundibugyo virus incubation-period estimate comes from the 2007 Uganda outbreak (mean 6.3 d, 95% CI 5.2-7.3)[82]. The generation interval is taken from the Ebola virus disease serial interval (mean 15.3 d, SD 9.3 d; WHO Ebola Response Team 2014)[83]. The CDC summary for the two previous BVD outbreaks gives a case-fatality figure with confidence bands[84] used to inform the CFR prior. A BEAST X reanalysis of 139 BDBV genomes reports an exponential-growth doubling time of 11.7 d (95% HPD 6.8-17.5)[16], and a BEAST time tree of the first ten sequenced genomes places the TMRCA at a mean of 25 March 2026[45]. Field epidemiology in Mongbwalu traced a sustained transmission chain back to a death on 25 January 2026, identifying more than 500 suspected cases between mid-January and mid-May (Kupferschmidt, 2026)[85].

Verheyden and Mudogo (27 Jul 2026)
Sixteen Days Undetected: Growth Dynamics and the Case for Pre-Positioned Response Capacity in the 2026 Bundibugyo Virus Disease¶

Outbreak, Democratic Republic of the Congo

Read the analysis

Overview¶

This analysis estimates the early exponential growth rate of the 2026 BVD outbreak in DRC, back-calculates when transmission likely began before international detection, and examines whether the observed rise in case fatality ratio reflects true severity change or a surveillance artefact. The authors analysed a corrected daily surveillance series of 65 observations spanning 14 May to 27 July 2026 using non-linear least-squares regression and a Bayesian Poisson growth model fitted by Markov chain Monte Carlo, with five sensitivity analyses.[4] The main findings are that early confirmed cases grew at a doubling time of 5.50 days — roughly three times faster than previous BDBV outbreaks — that transmission likely began around 19 April 2026, some 25 days before laboratory confirmation, and that the confirmed CFR rose from 12.1% to 44.3%, a trajectory the authors attribute to progressive ascertainment improvement rather than increasing virulence.[18]

Estimate¶

This analysis does not produce an estimate of true (undetected) outbreak size or a detection multiplier in the conventional sense. Its central estimates concern growth rate, doubling time, and the back-calculated onset date, rather than a ratio of estimated true cases to confirmed cases.

Fitted to the 12 pre-discontinuity daily observations (14–27 May), non-linear regression yielded r = 0.1261 per day (95% CI 0.0885–0.1636), a doubling time of 5.50 days (95% CI 4.24–7.83; R² = 0.867).[13] The Bayesian posterior growth rate, median r = 0.1334 per day (95% HDI 0.1022–0.1697), is broadly concordant (5.8% relative difference), providing cross-methodological validation.[86]

The Bayesian back-calculation places outbreak onset at 19 April 2026 (95% HDI 9–27 April) — 16 days before the WHO alert (5 May) and 25 days before laboratory confirmation (14 May); the posterior probability that transmission preceded the WHO alert exceeded 99.9%.[87]

The detection-lag cost is expressed not as a case-count multiplier but as case growth implied by the doubling time: at a doubling time of 5.5 days, the detection lag alone corresponds to approximately six-fold case growth before international response mechanisms activated; at the WHO alert date, the model implies 4–13 circulating cases (median 8); by declaration on 15 May, 20–38 cases (median 28).[11]

Over the full 65-observation series (14 May–27 July), growth rate fell to r = 0.0364 per day (Tᵈ = 19.02 days), and a logistic model was preferred by AIC (K ≈ 6,166), confirming substantial deceleration, though the authors treat this plateau estimate as provisional: successive one-week extensions of the series shifted the fitted asymptote from K ≈ 2,333 to K ≈ 3,002 to K ≈ 6,166 (29% then 105% change).[88]

Across the five sensitivity analyses, back-calculated onset ranges 17–22 April, consistent with the primary estimate (19 April, 95% HDI 9–27 April); SA-1 is the exception, both numerically unstable and pointing to a later onset.[89]

Methods¶

Non-linear least-squares exponential regression: The early-phase model, covering 14–27 May (pre-discontinuity), was fitted by non-linear least squares to 12 daily observations of cumulative confirmed cases modelled as C(t) = C₀·exp(r·t), where r is the exponential growth rate and doubling time Tᵈ = ln(2)/r; a logistic model was also fitted to the full 65-observation series and compared against the exponential model by Akaike Information Criterion.[90] This produces the headline growth rate, doubling time, and a provisional logistic final-size estimate (K) for the full series, though the authors caution strongly against using K as a reliable projection.

Bayesian hierarchical back-calculation: A Bayesian hierarchical model with a Poisson likelihood and weakly informative Normal priors, fitted by Markov Chain Monte Carlo in PyMC3, estimated growth rate r, initial case count C₀, and t_back — the number of days before the first situation report that transmission began — with full posterior uncertainty propagation.[91] This model is applied to the DRC national confirmed case series and is the basis for the back-calculated transmission onset date. Five pre-specified sensitivity analyses varying priors, fitting windows, and the observation-model distribution were all rerun on the corrected daily series.[92]

CFR trajectory analysis: CFR was calculated at each reporting date, and at the earliest date with disaggregated confirmed and suspected case and death data (21 May 2026), the confirmed and suspected CFR were compared by two-sample z-test; the temporal CFR trajectory was also examined for consistency with progressive reclassification of suspected deaths into the confirmed category versus an irregular pattern consistent with genuine severity change.[93] This analysis is applied to DRC national aggregate data and does not produce an outbreak size estimate but informs clinical resource planning.

Assumptions¶

Single index case and single spillover: Back-calculation assumes a single index case; multiple early spillover events (as suggested for the 2012 BDBV outbreak) would shift the estimated start date later, making 19 April a conservative (earlier) estimate under the single-introduction assumption.[94]

Exponential growth in the early phase: The model assumes the pre-discontinuity window (14–27 May) reflects a period of unconstrained exponential expansion. Cumulative case counts C(t) were modelled as C(t) = C₀·exp(r·t), where r is the exponential growth rate.[90] The logistic model, fitted to the full series, adds a carrying capacity K, but K estimates should be read with particular caution: this figure has more than doubled across two successive one-week extensions of the data window (2333→3002→6166) and is reported for model-comparison completeness, not as a dependable final-size projection.[95]

Bayesian prior specifications: Weakly informative priors were used: r ∼ Normal(0.13, 0.05), C₀ ∼ Normal(33, 10), σ ∼ HalfNormal(20).[96] The sensitivity of the back-calculated onset to these priors was tested; across SA-2, SA-3, and both SA-5 variants, back-calculated onset ranges 17–22 April, consistent with the primary estimate.[89]

Observation model: The model actually run uses a Normal likelihood with an independently estimated observation-noise scale (σ ∼ HalfNormal(20)) rather than a Poisson likelihood.[97] The robustness of this choice was tested with a Student-t likelihood: the Student-t sensitivity yielded posterior median r = 0.133 per day (95% HDI 0.102–0.171), with estimated degrees-of-freedom posterior median of 19, consistent with near-Normal behaviour — little evidence that heavy-tailed noise materially affects the primary estimate.[98]

CFR ascertainment assumption: The analysis assumes the observed CFR trajectory reflects progressive reclassification (ascertainment lag) rather than increasing virulence. This is interpreted as a testing-order effect: contact-tracing teams first reached surviving contacts, temporarily inflating the survivor share among confirmed cases; as testing capacity expanded, fatal cases previously counted as suspected were progressively confirmed and reclassified. This mechanism is independently corroborated by a surveillance-maturity discontinuity identified on 28 May 2026, externally confirmed by a documented Africa CDC-supported capacity-expansion plan two days earlier that deployed 36 additional PCR machines across 19 health zones.[99] CFR interpretation rests on aggregate surveillance data and a single cross-classification snapshot; line-list data stratified by onset date, confirmation date, care setting, and outcome would be needed to enable formal survival analysis.[24]

Exclusion of possible earlier Mongbwalu cluster: The analysis does not incorporate field and media reports of a possible earlier, undetected cluster of deaths in Mongbwalu health zone linked to a funeral held 3–4 February 2026; the authors treat this instead as an explicit plausibility bound — if this cluster reflects genuine early BDBV transmission, true onset could lie anywhere between early February 2026 and the estimated 19 April 2026.[100]

Limitations¶

Data series completeness and prior extraction errors: The original analysis relied on weekly aggregated case counts (n = 3 for the early-phase model); this has been resolved using the complete corrected daily surveillance series (12 pre-discontinuity observations, 65 in total). The daily series is not entirely complete: ten dates lack confirmed-case counts in the primary source and were excluded rather than interpolated — a larger set than an earlier draft reported (five dates through the previous 20 July cut-off).[101]

Approximate historical comparisons: Historical BDBV doubling-time comparisons are approximate; formal statistical comparison requires digitised onset curves from 2007 and 2012 primary sources, which are ongoing.[102]

Single-introduction back-calculation assumption: Back-calculation assumes a single index case; multiple early spillover events would shift the estimated start date later, making 19 April a conservative (earlier) estimate.[94]

Aggregate CFR data: CFR interpretation rests on aggregate surveillance data and a single cross-classification snapshot rather than line-list survival analysis.[24]

Inferential mechanistic discussion: The mechanistic discussion of growth-rate drivers is inferential; testing any individual mechanism requires appropriately controlled epidemiological studies.[103]

Unverified earlier Mongbwalu cluster: A co-investigator raised the possibility of an earlier, undetected cluster in Mongbwalu health zone during review; the authors report this evidence transparently but have not incorporated it into the back-calculation analysis, as doing so would require independent verification that lies beyond the scope of the present dataset.[104]

Unstable logistic final-size estimate: The logistic K figure should be read as illustrative of curve shape, not as a dependable final-size projection; the growth-rate and back-calculated-onset estimates, by contrast, are unaffected by any of the successive data extensions, since they derive solely from the closed pre-discontinuity window.[105]

Sensitivity analyses not fully robust: Results are broadly but not completely robust, with two of five variants implying a modestly later onset.[106]

Data sources¶

Primary outbreak data: Cumulative confirmed case counts and deaths were extracted from a corrected daily surveillance series (65 observations, 14 May–27 July 2026) drawn from the INRB-UMIE BDBV2026-Data repository of digitised DRC INSP situation reports; this corrected series superseded an earlier extraction from WHO AFRO Weekly External Situation Reports, which was found on reanalysis to contain date-alignment and transcription errors.[107] The series was extended through 27 July by aggregating the repository’s health-zone-level records to national daily totals; every resulting checkpoint was cross-validated against independently published figures (15 July: 2,124 cases/828 deaths, WHO Disease Outbreak News; 18 July: 2,344/930, NICD; 27 July: 3,360/1,487, ECDC).[108] Ten reporting dates (15–16 May, 12 June, 26 June, 28 June, 12 July, 14 July, 16 July, 21 July, and 24 July 2026) lack confirmed-case counts in the source and were excluded rather than interpolated.[109]

Auxiliary data: Epidemiological context and the 21 May 2026 cross-classification data were taken from Mwamba et al. and Tonen-Wolyec and Bélec.[110] Historical BDBV outbreak parameters for comparison purposes were drawn from the two prior outbreaks: the index Uganda epidemic (2007–2008; 116–149 cases; CFR 25–34%) and a subsequent epidemic in Isiro, DRC (2012; 52–62 cases; CFR 49–54%).[111] No travel data, demographic data, or formally elicited epidemiological parameters from external sources are used as model inputs; the Bayesian model uses weakly informative Normal priors specified by the authors.

Verheyden et al. (20 Jul 2026)
How Predictable Was the 2026 Bundibugyo Virus Disease Outbreak? A Rolling-Origin Evaluation of Short-Term Forecast Models, an Empirically Recalibrated Bayesian Model, and a Data-Driven Baseline–Bayesian Ensemble, Using Daily Surveillance Data¶

Read the analysis

Overview¶

This analysis assessed how accurately the 2026 BVD outbreak in DRC could have been forecast in real time using routinely published national situation reports, whether a simple ensemble of two complementary models improved on either alone, and how the resulting forecasts and their uncertainty should be interpreted for operational capacity planning.[112] At each forecast origin, two prespecified operational models were refitted using only data available at that time — a recent seven-increment baseline and a Bayesian negative-binomial surveillance-maturity model — alongside a Gompertz growth model fitted as a phenomenological benchmark.[113] The main finding is that routine SitRep data supported useful short-term forecasting, but no single model was best on every criterion, and a data-driven combination of two complementary models measurably outperformed either alone for one of the two outcomes evaluated.[114]

Estimate¶

This analysis is a forecasting evaluation study, not an outbreak size estimation study. It does not produce a model-based estimate of true (under-detected) outbreak size or a detection multiplier. The estimates reported are short-term forecasts of confirmed case and death counts forward from each rolling origin.

Prospective (not-yet-scoreable) forecasts from the most recent eligible origin of 20 July 2026 — at which point there were 2,473 cumulative confirmed cases and 999 cumulative confirmed deaths — are reported for 7-, 14-, and 21-day horizons.[115] The 21-day Bayesian death forecast (median 2,286.8, more than double the 999 deaths recorded at the origin) is flagged as an aggressive extrapolation that should be read as an upper scenario rather than a precise point estimate; the forecast-maturity ratio for this specific origin-horizon pair is 2.52 (mature), illustrating that a mature ratio constrains but does not eliminate long-horizon extrapolation risk.[116]

For validated rolling hindcast performance: for cases, the baseline retained the lowest or near-lowest median point error at every horizon (median absolute percentage error 3.2%, 5.9%, and 10.7% at 7, 14, and 21 days); the ensemble, at its evidence-selected baseline-heavy weighting (w=0.8–0.9), tracked the baseline’s point accuracy closely while modestly improving mean weighted interval score over the baseline alone at every horizon (7-day: 37.4→36.6; 14-day: 91.2→84.3; 21-day: 173.2→170.7).[117] For deaths, the ensemble’s evidence-selected near-parity weighting (w=0.5–0.6) produced a genuine three-way improvement in weighted interval score over both individual component models at every horizon (7-day: baseline 24.8, Bayesian 20.5, ensemble 17.9; 14-day: baseline 73.8, Bayesian 55.3, ensemble 45.1; 21-day: baseline 145.5, Bayesian 135.4, ensemble 95.2).[118]

Methods¶

Seven-increment recent-trend baseline: This model assumed that the recent mean reporting pace would continue over the forecast horizon. For valid one-calendar-day increments, the expected daily increment at each origin was the mean of the seven most recent valid increments, with the point forecast summed over the horizon. Predictive intervals were generated by bootstrap resampling of the recent valid increments (20,000 replicates), with resampled negative increments truncated at zero, using a deterministic origin-specific seed for reproducibility.[119] The model was applied at the national level using the full DRC SitRep series.

Bayesian negative-binomial surveillance-maturity model: An initial log-linear negative-binomial specification proved structurally inadequate once a surveillance-maturity discontinuity was identified on 28 May 2026, as a single trend line cannot simultaneously represent a step change in ascertainment and the underlying epidemic trajectory. It was replaced with a specification fitted by full Markov Chain Monte Carlo. The model included a baseline log-mean, a level shift for the 28 May discontinuity, separate trend slopes for pre- and post-discontinuity regimes, serial dependence on previous observed and expected counts (an INGARCH-type structure), and a negative-binomial dispersion parameter, with weakly informative priors throughout.[120] Rather than applying a single fixed historical-bias correction, a prospective, quality-gated recalibration was applied at every origin and horizon, using the median forecast error over all earlier origins at the same horizon that had already been observed and met a forecast-maturity criterion.[121] The model was applied at the national (DRC) level.

Gompertz growth model (benchmark, excluded): Cumulative cases or deaths were modelled using the Gompertz function, refitted at each origin by non-linear least squares subject to positivity constraints, with predictive uncertainty from parametric bootstrap. A fit was flagged unstable if the estimated asymptote exceeded 20 times the cumulative total at the origin. The model’s 80% predictive-interval coverage was the poorest of all candidates at every horizon and outcome (25.9–34.1% for cases, 0.0–23.5% for deaths) and is reported as tested and excluded rather than omitted.[122]

Data-driven ensemble: At each origin and horizon, a proportion w of a combined predictive sample was drawn from the baseline’s bootstrap trajectories and the remaining (1−w) from the Bayesian model’s recalibrated posterior predictive trajectories, with the ensemble’s median and predictive intervals computed directly from the pooled sample. The mixing weight w was selected separately for each outcome and horizon using a strictly prospective, expanding-origin procedure, minimising an operational loss function over all strictly earlier origins. The operational loss combined point accuracy with an explicit asymmetric capacity-planning penalty, with parameters λ=2 and γ=1 chosen for illustration.[123]

Assumptions¶

Baseline trend stationarity: The baseline model assumed that the recent mean reporting pace — defined as the mean of the seven most recent valid one-calendar-day increments — would continue unchanged over the forecast horizon.[124] This assumption is violated when reporting rates change abruptly, as occurred on 28 May.

Surveillance-maturity discontinuity date and parameterisation: The Bayesian model treats 28 May 2026 as a known, fixed changepoint date. The regime-split specification includes separate trend slopes for pre- and post-discontinuity periods and a level shift (ω₂ ∼ Normal(0, 2) under the prospective, no-lookahead scenario). Weakly informative priors are placed on all parameters; no prior information from other outbreaks is incorporated into the Bayesian model itself.[125][126]

Recalibration quality gate: The recalibration correction assumes that the median forecast error from earlier, forecast-mature origins is a valid correction for future bias. Where fewer than five reliable prior origins existed — consistently the case for the 21-day horizon early in the outbreak — no correction was applied, and this was recorded explicitly. This design guards against early-origin instability but means the correction is unavailable precisely when uncertainty is highest.[127]

Forecast-maturity threshold: The analysis assumes that a forecast-maturity ratio of ≥1 (mature surveillance history at least as long as the forecast horizon) is necessary for reliable forecasting. Absolute percentage error fell five- to sevenfold once this ratio reached 1, consistently across all three model architectures in this dataset.[128]

Asymmetric operational loss function: The ensemble weight-selection procedure uses an operational loss with parameters λ=2 and γ=1, reflecting a policy judgement that under-preparation is costlier than over-preparation. These values were chosen for illustration rather than derived from a documented cost structure.[129]

National aggregate data only: All models use only the national aggregate surveillance series, implicitly assuming that national trends are informative for planning; health-zone-level heterogeneity, which the underlying data show to be substantial, is not modelled.[130]

Limitations¶

Aggregate data only: All evaluated models used only the national aggregate series; health-zone-level heterogeneity, which the underlying surveillance data show to be substantial, was not modelled explicitly and is identified as a natural extension.[130]

Internal validation only for recalibration and ensemble weighting: The empirical recalibration and ensemble weighting procedures, though strictly prospective within this dataset, were both selected and validated using the same 55 origins reported in the results. Genuine held-out validation on a separate outbreak, as performed for the forecast-maturity relationship itself, was not attempted for these two specific procedures and would strengthen confidence in their generalisability.[131]

Illustrative cost parameters: The asymmetric operational loss function’s cost parameters (λ, γ) were chosen for illustration rather than derived from a documented capacity-planning cost structure; operational adopters should re-derive these from their own context.[132]

Residual long-horizon extrapolation risk: A forecast-maturity ratio at or above 1 constrains but does not eliminate the risk of aggressive long-horizon extrapolation from a still-evolving outbreak, and this risk should continue to be monitored and reported explicitly rather than assumed away by the maturity criterion alone.[133]

Data sources¶

Primary outbreak data: Daily cumulative confirmed cases and deaths were extracted from national situation reports published by the Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale (INRB) and cross-validated against independent contemporaneous sources (WHO Disease Outbreak News, Africa CDC situation updates, NICD, and ECDC epidemiological updates) where available. The analytical series spans 14 May to 20 July 2026 (68 calendar dates; 61 dates with a numeric national report).[134] All underlying surveillance data are publicly available without restriction from the INRB-UMIE BDBV2026-Data GitHub repository, accessed and archived on 20 July 2026.[135] Seven calendar dates lack a national confirmed-case observation (15–16 May, 12, 26, and 28 June, and 14 and 16 July) and are retained as explicitly missing rather than imputed or interpolated.[136]

Auxiliary data: A changepoint scan identified a discontinuity on 28 May 2026, with external corroboration from a documented Africa CDC surveillance-decentralisation plan two days prior, used to validate that the discontinuity reflects a change in case-ascertainment capacity rather than transmission alone.[137] The forecast-maturity relationship was cross-validated in an independent completed 77-week outbreak (North Kivu/Ituri, 2018–2020) using a deliberately simpler method. At a 28-day horizon, no origin in the current dataset has yet accumulated sufficient mature history. At a 21-day horizon, the ratio first reaches 1 at the 18 June origin, and 33 of 55 origins qualify as forecast-mature by 20 July.[138] No individual-level line list data, travel data, or historical outbreak parameter sets are used as model inputs.

Kim et al. (21 Jun 2026)
Cross-border travel patterns affect magnitude estimates for the Ebola Bundibugyo epidemic¶

Read the analysis

Overview¶

This analysis estimates an upper bound on the likely burden of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) early in the 2026 epidemic, based on the number of cases imported and confirmed in Uganda.[139] It expands a geographic spread approach to account for two specific contextual factors: that most cross-border movements between DRC and Uganda are short-duration trips, and that all cases imported and confirmed in Uganda were individuals who travelled specifically to seek healthcare.[140] Incorporating these factors substantially affected burden estimates, highlighting both the potential severity of the epidemic in its early phase and the critical need to consider local epidemiological contexts when applying geographic spread approaches to reduce and be aware of potential biases in estimates for early epidemic responses.[141]

Estimate¶

The analysis reports estimates under multiple scenarios combining source population scope (Ituri alone vs. Ituri and Nord Kivu), number of assumed imported cases (3 vs. 0, the latter after excluding healthcare-seeking travellers), and travel-duration accounting (with vs. without). Table 1 in the paper presents estimates and 95% confidence intervals of the number of BVD cases in the DRC across these combinations, but the full numerical table is not included in the document as provided.[142]

Accounting for the observed pattern of trip durations with three imported cases substantially increased central estimates and widened 95% confidence intervals compared to not accounting for travel durations within the framework and to estimates reported by McCabe et al.[8] Under the zero-imported-cases scenario (after excluding healthcare-seeking travellers), central estimates and lower confidence limits were zero by definition; however, the upper confidence limits provided informative likely upper bounds for early BVD burden, intended for use in epidemic response planning.[9] The interpretation offered is that if true BVD cases in the DRC were higher than these upper limits, non-zero imported cases would have been expected among individuals travelling to Uganda for general purposes.[143] Specific numerical values for the central estimates and confidence intervals by scenario are not recoverable from the text of the document provided.

Methods¶

Geographic spread back-calculation with travel-duration adjustment: This approach estimates the total number of BVD cases in the DRC source population by working backwards from the count of cases exported to and detected in Uganda, divided by the probability that an infected traveller would actually be detected while in Uganda. The method obtains the overall probability of detection while travelling as a weighted average over different durations of travel and different infection-to-detection intervals.[144] Travel duration data from the March 2020 IOM Uganda–DRC Border Flow Monitoring Dashboard were used for the baseline scenario, reclassified into three categories: less than 1 day (64.7%), 1 day to 1 week (25.9%), and longer than 1 week (9.4%).[145] The number of exported cases was divided by the overall probability of detection to estimate DRC cases, with 95% confidence intervals derived from the Poisson-likelihood-based confidence limits for the rate of exported cases — for example, the 95% CI for zero exported cases is (0, 1.92).[146] The method was applied to both the Ituri and Ituri-plus-Nord-Kivu source populations.

The analysis runs two principal scenarios regarding the number of imported cases to use as the numerator. With three imported cases and accounting for the observed pattern of trip durations, central estimates were substantially higher and confidence intervals wider compared to not accounting for travel durations.[8] With zero imported cases — that is, after excluding all three imported cases because their travel was healthcare-seeking — central estimates and lower confidence limits were uninformative (zero by definition), but upper confidence limits provided informative likely upper bounds for early BVD burden.[9] A sensitivity scenario used April 2019 IOM data with a different travel-duration distribution: less than 1 day (47.4%), 1 day to 1 week (45.4%), and longer than 1 week (7.2%).[147]

Assumptions¶

Healthcare-seeking travel and the equal-travel assumption: The conventional geographic spread approach assumes individuals in the source population have an equal probability of travelling regardless of infection status; the analysis identifies this as violated in the DRC–Uganda context because all confirmed imported cases were healthcare-seeking travellers, meaning that excluding healthcare travel, there had been no confirmed imported cases in Uganda through 21 June 2026.[148] This motivates the zero-imported-cases scenario as the preferred structural framing, with three imported cases treated as a comparison.

Travel duration distributions: The baseline assumes trip-duration proportions from the March 2020 IOM Dashboard (90.6% of trips lasting a week or less, 64.7% day trips); the alternative scenario uses April 2019 IOM data (92.8% lasting a week or less). Trip-duration data were not available for the period when early imported cases were confirmed in Uganda; short-duration trips are considered to have dominated cross-border movement during this period.[149]

Infection-to-detection interval: The delay from infection to detection is modelled with a Gamma distribution (shape 2.52, rate 0.40) for the incubation period, shifted by an assumed onset-to-detection delay to produce median infection-to-detection intervals of 10, 15, and 20 days, following McCabe et al.[150] The analysis acknowledges that the time from infection to detection varies between individuals depending on biological and behavioural factors as well as healthcare availability for clinical assessment and diagnostic testing.[151]

Fixed travel durations within categories: Within the less-than-1-day and 1-day-to-1-week categories, fixed median travel durations of 0.5 and 4 days are assigned respectively; travellers in the longer-than-1-week category are assumed to remain in Uganda indefinitely — long enough to be detected there.[152]

Source population and proportionality: Estimates are expected to change proportionally to the assumed source population size and could be biased if assumed source population sizes did not accurately reflect the catchment population of those travelling to Uganda, since residents near the DRC–Uganda border likely have substantially different travel probabilities than those living further away, particularly given that border communities operate as dynamic and shared economic entities.[153]

Reduced travel probability among the infected: If infected individuals were less likely to travel for non-healthcare-seeking purposes — for example due to feeling poorly — the burden estimate would scale up according to the inverse of the factor by which they were less likely to travel.[154]

Limitations¶

Violation of the equal-travel assumption: The standard geographic spread approach assumes individuals have an equal probability of travelling regardless of infection status. This assumption is violated because all imported cases confirmed in Uganda were healthcare-seeking travellers, meaning the observed exported cases cannot serve as a representative signal of background travel.[27][155]

Unavailability of contemporaneous trip-duration data: Trip-duration data were not available for the period when early imported cases were confirmed in Uganda, requiring the analysis to rely on 2019 and 2020 IOM data as proxies. Short-duration trips are considered to have dominated cross-border movement during this period, but this is based on expert communication rather than direct measurement.[156]

Source population size uncertainty: Estimates are expected to change proportionally to the assumed source population size and could be biased if these sizes did not accurately reflect the catchment population of those travelling to Uganda. Those residing near the border probably have substantially different travel probabilities, and individuals who can afford to travel to seek healthcare abroad may also have different baseline infection risks compared with the general population.[157][158]

Uninformative lower bound under the zero-imported-cases scenario: When zero imported cases are used — the scenario reflecting the exclusion of healthcare-seeking travellers — central estimates and lower confidence limits are zero by definition, meaning the approach can only provide informative upper bounds rather than a full distributional estimate of true burden.[9]

Knowledge gap on cross-border dynamics: A better understanding of the complex cross-border crossing dynamics would be needed to obtain more robust estimates of true case burden using this approach.[159]

Data sources¶

Primary outbreak data: All 15 BVD cases imported and confirmed in Uganda through 21 June 2026, all of whom were Congolese nationals who came to Uganda to seek medical care, form the primary signal for the back-calculation.[160] The first three confirmed imported cases, available by 9 June 2026 when McCabe et al. was published, are the specific numerator used in the three-imported-cases scenario.[155]

Auxiliary data: Cross-border travel duration distributions come from the March 2020 IOM Uganda–DRC Border Flow Monitoring Dashboard (baseline scenario), providing proportions for less than 1 day (64.7%), 1 day to 1 week (25.9%), and longer than 1 week (9.4%).[145] The April 2019 IOM Uganda–DRC Border Flow Monitoring Dashboard provides an alternative travel-duration distribution used in the sensitivity scenario.[147] Daily traveller counts and source population sizes for Ituri (1,871 travellers/day; population 4,392,200) and Ituri plus Nord Kivu (4,339 travellers/day; population 13,392,200) were taken directly from McCabe et al.[161][162] The incubation period was modelled using a Gamma distribution (shape 2.52, rate 0.40) to derive infection-to-detection intervals with median times of 10, 15, and 20 days, following McCabe et al.[150]

Epistorm (21 Jun 2026)
Ebola Bundibugyo Virus — DRC · Spread Risk Assessment #5 · Local Transmission Scenarios¶

Read the analysis

Overview¶

This analysis estimates the burden of the Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in Ituri Province, DRC, and projects forward trajectories under three counterfactual isolation scenarios. It uses a stochastic, metapopulation transmission model built on the GLEAM framework, incorporating transmission in the hospital, community, and through funerals, and explicitly modelling isolation protocols through Ebola treatment centres.[163] The model yields a posterior R0 of 2.34 (90% CrI 1.83 to 3.08); under 75% isolation, median cumulative cases in Ituri reach 2,509 (90% CrI 1,053 to 4,688) by 24 June 2026, and the probability of exceeding 20,000 cumulative cases by 31 August 2026 ranges from 45% (50% isolation) to 0% (95% isolation).[164]

Estimate¶

The analysis reports estimates for Ituri Province only across two snapshot dates and three forward scenarios.

Posterior snapshot at 24 May 2026: The filtered posterior predictive distribution of cumulative symptomatic cases in Ituri on 24 May 2026 has a median of 757 and a 90% credible interval of 378 to 1,298.[165]

Forward projection at 24 June 2026 (75% isolation, primary scenario): Median cumulative symptomatic cases 2,509 (90% CrI 1,053 to 4,688); active cases (community + HCF + ETC) 541 (90% CrI 189 to 1,260); new symptomatic cases per day 52 (90% CrI 15 to 137).[166]

Scenario outcomes by 31 August 2026: The probability that cumulative symptomatic cases in Ituri exceed 10,000 is 70% under 50% isolation, 21% under 75%, and 0% under 95%; for the higher threshold of at least 20,000 cases, the corresponding probabilities are 45%, 3%, and 0%.[167] The primary driver of the spread across scenarios is the isolation rate: strong isolation drives the outbreak to extinction by end of August, while a slip to 50% leaves it uncontrolled.[168]

The analysis does not provide a single headline under-detection multiplier comparing estimated true cases to confirmed cases, but the calibration window implies a maximum multiplier of up to 5× at the 13 June 2026 cutoff (ascertainment as low as 20% means up to five true cases per confirmed).

Methods¶

GLEAM stochastic metapopulation model with care-pathway SEIHFR: This is a stochastic metapopulation transmission model built on the GLEAM framework, incorporating transmission in the hospital, community, and through funerals, and explicitly modelling isolation protocols through Ebola treatment centres.[163] The framework couples an Africa-wide metapopulation network by daily commuting matrices and origin-destination passenger flows from IATA Passenger Intelligence Services and OAG Aviation Analytics.[169] The compartmental structure follows a Legrand-like SEIHFR scheme, with three potential outcomes at symptom onset modelling the impact of isolation and safe-burial protocols.[170] The model is applied to Ituri Province as the primary estimation geography, with seeding there and spread to other basins only through mobility coupling.

Two-stage Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) calibration: The model is calibrated by ABC in two stages: Stage 1 conditions on observed cross-border importations from Ituri to Uganda (exactly one importation by 14 May and one further importation 14–18 May 2026); Stage 2 conditions the Stage-1 posterior on the cumulative laboratory-confirmed count in Ituri at 13 June 2026 (717 cases), allowing ascertainment as low as 20%, requiring simulated cumulative symptomatic onsets to lie in the window 717 to 3,585.[171] The baseline allows ascertainment as low as 20%; sensitivity runs relax this to 15% (window 717 to 4,780) or 10% (window 717 to 7,170).[172]

Scenario projections under three isolation rates: Forward projections evaluate three target isolation rates (50%, 75%, and 95%), each phased in at 10 percentage points every 2 days from 15 May 2026 in Ituri Province.[173] These scenarios produce the headline outcome distributions for cumulative and active cases through 31 August 2026.

Assumptions¶

Ascertainment and calibration window: The Stage-2 evidence filter requires that simulated cumulative symptomatic onsets in Ituri by 13 June 2026 lie in the window 717 to 3,585, allowing ascertainment as low as 20%.[2] The baseline uses a 20% floor; sensitivity runs allow floors of 15% (window 717 to 4,780) and 10% (window 717 to 7,170).[172] Posterior medians are stable across the three floors (R0 shifts by about 4%, doubling time by about 3%), but the upper credible-interval bounds tighten as the floor rises.[174][175]

Reproduction number and epidemic seed: The accepted posterior yields a median R0 of 2.34 (90% CrI 1.83 to 3.08) and a median empirical doubling time of 10.6 days (90% CrI 8.5 to 13.5).[14] The epidemic is seeded with 5 infectious cases in Ituri on the inferred start date; every other basin begins fully susceptible and is reached only through mobility coupling.[176]

Care-pathway and isolation timings: Routine HCF cases are assumed to be infectious for an average of 5 days before admission; isolation-track cases are infectious for an average of 2 days before being moved to a HCF for 3 days, then to an ETC where transmission stops.[177] Isolation-pathway timings (2 days to HCF, approximately 3 days HCF-to-ETC) are based on the 2018 North Kivu RVEAP response, which may not exactly match 2026 operational reality.[178][179] A residual nosocomial channel of 10% of the baseline HCF rate is retained during the HCF-to-ETC transit, reflecting imperfect IPC during transfer; this is a modelling assumption that is sensitivity-testable.[180][181]

Isolation scenario structure: The three scenarios (50%, 75%, 95%) are each phased in at 10 percentage points every 2 days from 15 May 2026.[173] The isolation ramp and case-finding timings are applied homogeneously across all symptomatic cases, whereas real-world coverage varies by location and over time.[182]

Mobility: No mobility reductions between subpopulations are assumed: no behavioural reduction and no border closure are explicitly modelled.[183] Mobility is held static across the simulation, with no seasonality in transmissibility, and informal cross-border movement may be under-captured.[184]

Calibration targets: Stage 1 uses only evidence of Ituri-to-Uganda importations with no tolerance band; within-Ituri incidence is not directly fit in Stage 1. Stage 2 adds a single cumulative count at one date. Alternative acceptance rules or additional within-basin time points would shift the posteriors.[185]

Limitations¶

Calibration on sparse data: Stage 1 uses only two importation events with exact counts and no tolerance band, and Stage 2 adds only a single cumulative count at one date. The authors note that alternative acceptance rules or additional within-basin time points would shift the posteriors.[185]

Geographic scope restricted to Ituri: All figures and statistics are for Ituri Province only; cross-basin spillover to North Kivu, Uganda, Rwanda, and elsewhere is not reported in this analysis.[186]

Homogeneous and static isolation assumption: The isolation ramp and case-finding timings are applied homogeneously across all symptomatic cases, whereas real-world coverage varies by location and over time.[182]

Static mobility with possible under-capture of informal movement: Mobility is held static across the simulation, with no behavioural reduction, no border closure modelled, and no seasonality in transmissibility. The authors note that informal cross-border movement may be under-captured.[184]

Care-pathway parameters from a different response context: Isolation-track timings (2 days onset-to-HCF, approximately 3 days HCF-to-ETC) follow the 2018 North Kivu RVEAP response, which may not exactly match 2026 operational reality.[179]

Projections are model-driven beyond the calibration date: Calibration extends only to the 13 June 2026 confirmed-case evidence; projections beyond that date are model-driven and depend on assumptions about isolation timing and intensity.[187]

Data sources¶

Primary outbreak data: The Stage-2 calibration target is the cumulative laboratory-confirmed count in Ituri at 13 June 2026, reported as 717 cases.[2] The situational context draws on the 21 June 2026 DRC-wide surveillance snapshot of 1,048 laboratory-confirmed cases and 267 confirmed deaths across 34 health zones.[188] Uganda’s 20 laboratory-confirmed cases including 2 deaths are also noted as context.[189] The Stage-1 calibration uses observed cross-border importation counts from Ituri to Uganda: exactly one importation by 14 May 2026 and one further importation in the window 14–18 May 2026.[190]

Auxiliary data — mobility: Daily commuting matrices and origin-destination passenger flows come from IATA Passenger Intelligence Services and OAG Aviation Analytics.[169]

Auxiliary data — natural history and compartmental parameters: The Legrand-type SEIHFR formulation supplies the framework; Wamala et al. are the source for the original 2007–2008 Uganda BVD outbreak data on which some BVD-specific natural-history estimates rest.[191] Isolation-pathway case-finding timings follow the 2018 North Kivu RVEAP response.[178]

Chamla et al. (8 Jun 2026)
Size of the 2026 Ebola outbreak and risk of cross-border spillover from Bundibugyo virus in Ituri Province, DR Congo, and its implications for preparedness: a recalibrated stochastic modelling study¶

Read the analysis

Overview¶

This analysis estimates the short-term epidemic trajectory of the 2026 BDBV outbreak in Ituri Province, DRC, and the probability of cross-border spillover into neighbouring countries. It uses a stochastic SEIRD (susceptible, exposed, infectious, recovered, dead) ensemble model calibrated to 598 cumulative laboratory-confirmed cases as of 8 June 2026, with simulation filtering to retain model runs consistent with that anchor.[192] Under the central scenario (R0 = 1.71), the model projects a median of 990 cumulative confirmed cases by week 12 (24 June 2026; 90% prediction interval 709 to 1,293) and 174 deaths, with cross-border importation into Uganda assessed as nearly certain (94.2%) and into South Sudan as highly probable (69.3%).[193]

Estimate¶

Under the central transmissibility scenario (mean accepted R0 = 1.71), the ensemble projected a median of 648 cumulative confirmed cases by week 10 (8 June 2026; 50% PI 560 to 732), rising to 990 by week 12 (24 June 2026; 50% PI 858 to 1,141 and 90% PI 709 to 1,293), with a projected median of 174 deaths at week 12.[15]

Under the low-transmissibility scenario (mean accepted R0 = 1.42), cumulative confirmed cases reached a median of 870 by week 12 (50% PI 752 to 1,004 and 90% PI 641 to 1,133; 160 deaths) and 3,662 by week 24 (50% PI 2,884 to 4,484 and 90% PI 2,094 to 6,037; 673 deaths).[194]

Under the high-transmissibility scenario (mean accepted R0 = 2.08), confirmed cases reached a median of 1,364 (50% PI 1,154 to 1,579 and 90% PI 975 to 1,807; 202 deaths) by week 12, rising to 66,420 (50% PI 56,560 to 78,937 and 90% PI 41,718 to 95,881; 10,644 deaths) by week 24.[195]

Under the central scenario, week 24 projects a median of 8,210 cumulative confirmed cases (50% PI 6,636 to 10,287 and 90% PI 5,063 to 13,498) and approximately 1,440 deaths if transmission were merely sustained.[196]

The observed confirmed-case trajectory is consistent with the central scenario; the high scenario is retained as an upper-bound contingency should control measures lapse.[197] Importantly, this analysis calibrates exclusively to laboratory-confirmed cases and does not produce a separate “true outbreak size” estimate that exceeds the confirmed count; the reporting fraction was set at 1.0 because laboratory-confirmed cases are, by definition, ascertained, and the earlier suspected-case reporting fraction assumption is no longer required.[10] No detection multiplier is calculated or reported.

Methods¶

Stochastic SEIRD ensemble model: A discrete-time SEIRD framework with daily transitions implemented as binomial draws using standard mass-action incidence, applied to the DRC outbreak (Ituri and Nord Kivu provinces combined). Three transmissibility scenarios span published BDBV estimates: low R0 = 1.42, central R0 = 1.71, and high R0 = 2.08.[198][199][200] Calibration was performed by simulation filtering (approximate rejection sampling, not formal Bayesian inference): replicates were accepted if cumulative laboratory-confirmed cases at day 68 (8 June 2026) fell within ±30% of 598 (range 419 to 777), retaining 400 calibration-passing replicates per scenario.[201] Sensitivity analyses examined travel-while-infectious (5% to 25%), reporting completeness (0.60 to 0.90), and catchment size (250,000 to 500,000).[202]

Daily-hazard spillover model: Importation risk to Uganda, South Sudan, Rwanda, and Burundi was modelled as a daily Poisson hazard driven by calibrated infectious prevalence from the SEIRD model, country-specific cross-border mobility, point-of-entry detection sensitivity from WHO Joint External Evaluation assessments, and travel-while-infectious parameters (Uganda 12%; South Sudan 15%; Rwanda and Burundi 8%), with full equations and parameter values given in an appendix.[203] Importation probability was computed as 1 − exp(cumulative 12-week hazard), yielding the probability of at least one importation for each country.[204]

Assumptions¶

Transmissibility scenarios: Three R0 values (low 1.42, central 1.71, high 2.08) span published BDBV estimates. Response-intensity reductions applied from 15 May 2026 are 20% (low scenario), 25% (central), and 15% (high), reflecting differing assumptions about operational effectiveness.[200][205]

Latent and infectious periods: The latent period is fixed at 9.7 days and the infectious period at 5.0 days, in line with the broader filovirus literature. These are not varied across scenarios.[206]

Case-fatality ratio: Drawn from a uniform distribution (0.15 to 0.25), centred on the observed confirmed-case ratio of approximately 19% (115 of 598 as of 8 June 2026) and consistent with the historical BDBV range.[207]

Ascertainment and reporting fraction: Set at 1.0 for laboratory-confirmed cases on the structural assumption that confirmed cases are fully ascertained by definition. This eliminates the need to estimate an under-detection multiplier but means the model tracks the confirmed trajectory only, not total infections.[10]

Homogeneous mixing and catchment size: The model assumes homogeneous mixing within a single catchment of 350,000 across seven affected health zones, including Ituri and Nord Kivu. Spatial heterogeneity is not captured, acknowledged by the authors as a stated limitation.[208]

Calibration tolerance: Simulation filtering accepts replicates if cumulative confirmed cases at day 68 fall within ±30% of 598 (range 419 to 777). The ±30% tolerance was chosen pragmatically given residual data uncertainty, and is not derived from formal inference.[209][210]

Cross-border mobility and travel-while-infectious parameters: The spillover model uses country-specific travel-while-infectious parameters (Uganda 12%; South Sudan 15%; Rwanda and Burundi 8%) alongside WHO Joint External Evaluation-based detection sensitivity. The authors acknowledge these parameters were not empirically derived for this outbreak and represent the principal sources of uncertainty in spillover projections.[211][212]

No vaccination compartment: No vaccinated compartment was included, reflecting the absence of a licensed BDBV-specific vaccine.[213]

Model type: These projections are described by the authors as exploratory preparedness-oriented estimates derived from a stochastic scenario-based modelling framework, rather than predictions generated from formally fitted epidemiological models using comprehensive parameter estimation and identifiability analyses.[214]

Limitations¶

Homogeneous mixing and absent spatial structure: The model oversimplifies spatial heterogeneity across health zones, does not separately model healthcare-worker transmission, and applies response intensity uniformly rather than varying it by place, time, access, or community acceptance.[215]

Single-point calibration anchor: The model is anchored on a single recent confirmed-case datum (598 on 8 June 2026), making the fit sensitive to that anchor.[215]

Simulation filtering is not formal inference: Calibration by approximate rejection sampling is acknowledged as not constituting formal Bayesian inference, and informal cross-border mobility estimates are described as imprecise.[215]

Uniform and static response intensity: The response-intensity factor was applied uniformly from 15 May, but real-world response effectiveness varies by place, time, access, and community acceptance. Live mobility data and behavioural adaptation were not incorporated.[216]

Surveillance dynamics and residual confounding: The post-declaration case-finding surge probably contributed to rapid apparent growth between 15 and 19 May; the analysis addressed this by lowering the reporting fraction and widening the calibration window, but residual confounding between transmission intensity and surveillance intensity remains.[217]

Early-phase data quality: Calibration initially relied on early-phase surveillance counts from the first weekly WHO External Situation Report, where the suspected-case total was only partially resolved into laboratory-confirmed cases and death counts reflected surveillance signals rather than confirmed mortality alone. Misclassification, delayed laboratory throughput, and ongoing active case finding could each shift the calibration anchor in either direction. The projections are therefore interpreted as an early situational assessment rather than a definitive forecast.[218]

Need for iterative recalibration: The projections require iterative recalibration as new data emerge.[32]

Data sources¶

Primary outbreak data: Case data were taken from WHO AFRO External Situation Reports and the WHO AFRO internal tracker through 8 June 2026. The laboratory-confirmed case series used as the primary calibration metric ran from 33 cases on 18 May 2026 to 105 on 24 May 2026 and 598 on 8 June 2026.[219] WHO External Situation Report 01 (as of 18 May 2026) documented 528 cumulative suspected cases, 132 deaths, and 35 laboratory-confirmed cases across DRC and Uganda.[220] Uganda’s confirmed case count of 19 as of 4 June 2026 (including five healthcare-worker infections and two deaths) is used to validate the spillover model output.[221]

Auxiliary data: Transmissibility scenario ranges were chosen to span published BDBV estimates from the 2007 Uganda and 2012 DRC outbreaks. The latent period was fixed at 9.7 days and the infectious period at 5.0 days, in line with the broader filovirus literature. The CFR was drawn from a uniform distribution (0.15 to 0.25), centred on the observed confirmed-case ratio of approximately 19% (115 of 598 as of 8 June 2026) and consistent with the historical BDBV range.[20] Point-of-entry detection sensitivity values for the spillover model were drawn from WHO Joint External Evaluation assessments; travel-while-infectious parameters (Uganda 12%; South Sudan 15%; Rwanda and Burundi 8%) were applied country-specifically.[211] Published reproduction number estimates from previous BDBV outbreaks in Uganda (2007) and DRC (2012), ranging from 1.2 to 2.6, informed scenario boundaries.[222]

McCabe et al. (27 May 2026)
Estimation of the Ebola outbreak size in the Democratic Republic of the Congo¶

Read the analysis

Overview¶

This analysis produces early estimates of the epidemic size in the Democratic Republic of the Congo as of May 27, 2026, using two independent, scenario-based methods applied under plausible assumptions about surveillance, severity, and epidemic growth.[1] The first method back-calculates cases from reported deaths using historical case fatality ratios and onset-to-death delays; the second estimates outbreak size from confirmed imported cases in Uganda combined with cross-border travel volumes. The two methods yield broadly consistent results, suggesting that approximately 280–2,520 cases of Bundibugyo virus disease may have occurred in DRC as of May 27, 2026.[5]

Estimate¶

Back-calculation from deaths: Assuming 30% of suspected and confirmed deaths are due to Ebola, a CFR of 33%, and a doubling time of 10 days, the mean estimated outbreak size is 451 cases (95% CI 396–511) as of May 27, 2026.[223] The estimated outbreak size increases with assumptions of a higher proportion of deaths due to Ebola, a lower CFR, and faster epidemic growth.[224] The full scenario range for this method is 306–2,521 cases.[5]
